title: Buxa Fort and the Duar War of 1864–65
meta_description: How Bhutan lost the Dooars: the eighteen passes, the Eden mission, the Duar War of 1864–65, the Treaty of Sinchula and Buxa Fort's later life as a prison.
summary: Until 1865 the Bengal Dooars belonged to Bhutan. A failed British mission in 1864, a short war over the winter of 1864–65 and the Treaty of Sinchula in November 1865 moved the plains to British India. Buxa Fort, on one of the old passes, saw it all, then became a prison and a refuge.

sections.heading: Eighteen doors into Bhutan
paras: The word Dooars comes from duar, door. Along the foot of the Himalaya between the Teesta and the Dhansiri, eighteen river gaps and passes led from the plains up into Bhutan. Through them came wool, rock salt, musk, ponies and cloth from the hills and from Tibet beyond; up them went rice, dried fish, cotton and silk. Whoever held the passes held that trade. Buxa Duar, north of today's Alipurduar, was one of the most important, on a route that ran up through the hills towards Punakha and on to Tibet.

By the eighteenth century Bhutan controlled most of these plains through its regional governors, the penlops, and local officers on the ground. The plains were split into the Bengal Duars in the west, between the Teesta and the Sankosh, and the Assam Duars in the east. The Rajbanshi, Mech, Rabha and Toto communities lived here long before any of the powers that fought over the land.

sections.heading: Friction on the Cooch Behar border
paras: The first clash with the British came through Cooch Behar, the Koch kingdom just south of the Dooars. In 1772, with Bhutanese forces involved in a succession struggle there, Cooch Behar asked the East India Company for help. Company troops pushed the Bhutanese back into the hills and took Buxa Fort. A treaty in 1774 restored the fort and the Dooars to Bhutan in return for peace on the border.

For the next seventy years the frontier stayed tense. Raids and counter-raids, disputes over runaway subjects and captives, and arguments about revenue from the Duars were common. In 1841 the British annexed the Assam Duars and agreed to pay Bhutan an annual sum in return. The Bengal Duars, including Buxa, stayed Bhutanese.

sections.heading: The Eden mission and the war
paras: In 1863 the government of India sent Ashley Eden to Bhutan to settle the border disputes and secure the return of captives. The mission reached Punakha in 1864 and went badly. Eden later said he had been insulted and forced to sign an agreement under pressure, which the British government disowned. In November 1864 Britain declared war and annexed the Bengal Duars by proclamation.

Four columns of what was called the Duar Field Force marched into the foothills that winter. Buxa and the western passes were taken quickly. In the east the fighting was harder. Bhutanese forces, led among others by the Trongsa Penlop Jigme Namgyal, father of Bhutan's first king, drove the British garrison out of Dewangiri in early 1865 before it was retaken. Disease, heavy rain and difficult ground hurt both sides. By mid-1865 the British held the passes, and Bhutan agreed to talk.

sections.heading: The Treaty of Sinchula, 1865
paras: The treaty was signed at Sinchula, in the hills above Buxa, on 11 November 1865. Bhutan ceded the Bengal Duars and the Assam Duars for good, along with a strip of hill territory east of the Teesta that included Kalimpong. In return the British agreed to pay Bhutan an annual allowance, beginning at ₹25,000 and rising in stages to ₹50,000, as long as Bhutan kept the treaty. The treaty also covered extradition of criminals and free trade between the two sides.

Kalimpong, ceded under this treaty, was joined first to the Western Duars and then, in 1866, to Darjeeling district. The Treaty of Punakha in 1910 raised the allowance to ₹1,00,000 and placed Bhutan's foreign relations under British guidance. After 1947 the 1949 Indo-Bhutan treaty took that role.

The Dooars changed fast after 1865. The forests were surveyed and reserved, the first tea garden opened at Gazaldoba in 1874, and by 1881 there were 55 gardens. Workers came from Chota Nagpur, Nepal and elsewhere, and a railway followed. Much of what a visitor sees today, from the tea lines to the forest boundaries, dates from the years after the treaty.

sections.heading: From pass fort to prison and refuge
paras: The British rebuilt Buxa Fort in brick and stone, and after the war it became a quiet frontier post. Its isolation later made it useful for another purpose. From 1930 to 1937 it was a detention camp for Indian revolutionaries held without trial under Bengal's emergency laws, kept far from their supporters in Calcutta and the districts. It was used again as a special jail in the 1940s and early 1950s. Rabindranath Tagore wrote verses for the detainees, which are remembered at the fort.

In 1959, after the Dalai Lama fled Tibet, the Indian government gave the fort and its barracks to refugee monks. Monks of Drepung and other great monasteries ran a study centre here, known as Buxa Chogar, keeping their teaching and debate traditions alive in the heat and damp. In 1971 they moved to new settlements in Karnataka, where the rebuilt monasteries stand today.

sections.heading: Visiting Buxa Fort today
paras: The fort is inside Buxa Tiger Reserve, about 15 km north of Rajabhatkhawa. Cars stop at Santalabari, and a stony path climbs through forest to the fort, about an hour on foot. Little remains: sections of wall, the gate area and a memorial to the detainees. The setting and the story are the reason to come. Above the fort, the Drukpa village of Lepchakha has a chorten and a wide view over the plains on a clear day.
Go with a local guide who can tell the fort's story; most of the ruins carry no signs. Pay the forest entry at Rajabhatkhawa and carry water, as there is little on the path.
list: Best months: October to April; the path is slippery and leech-ridden in the monsoon.
Time needed: half a day for the fort, a full day or an overnight with Lepchakha.
Cost: forest entry about ₹50–200 per person and a guide about ₹500–1,000 per group, indicative 2026.
Rules on entry and homestays inside the reserve change; check current status before you travel.

faqs.a: The Duar War, also called the Anglo-Bhutan War, was fought between British India and Bhutan from November 1864 to 1865. It followed the failed Ashley Eden mission to Punakha in 1864 and long-running border disputes. British columns took the passes into Bhutan, and the war ended with the Treaty of Sinchula on 11 November 1865.

faqs.q: What did the Treaty of Sinchula give Britain
faqs.a: Under the Treaty of Sinchula, Bhutan ceded the Bengal Duars and the Assam Duars, together with hill territory east of the Teesta including Kalimpong. In return Britain paid Bhutan an annual allowance that began at ₹25,000 and rose to ₹50,000. The treaty also dealt with trade and the return of criminals.

faqs.q: Why is the region called the Dooars
faqs.a: Dooars comes from duar, meaning door. Eighteen passes or river gaps once led from these plains into the hills of Bhutan, and the plains in front of them took the name. Buxa Duar was one of the best known, guarded by Buxa Fort.

The fort was originally a Bhutanese post guarding the Buxa Duar pass. The British took it in 1772, returned it under the 1774 treaty, and took it again in the Duar War of 1864–65. They later rebuilt it in brick and stone, and it is these later walls whose ruins you see today.

faqs.q: Why was Buxa Fort used as a prison
faqs.a: Its remoteness. From 1930 to 1937 the British used Buxa as a detention camp for Indian revolutionaries held without trial, far from their supporters in Bengal. It was used as a special jail again in the 1940s and early 1950s. A memorial at the fort remembers the detainees.

faqs.q: Did Tibetan monks live at Buxa
faqs.a: Yes. From 1959 to 1971, monks who had fled Tibet, many from Drepung Monastery, ran a study centre called Buxa Chogar in the old fort and barracks. In 1971 they moved to new settlements in Karnataka, where the large monasteries in exile now stand.

faqs.q: How do I get to Buxa Fort
faqs.a: Drive to Rajabhatkhawa, about 15 km north of Alipurduar town, pay the forest entry, and continue to Santalabari, where the road ends. From there a stony path climbs to the fort in about an hour. Alipurduar Junction is the nearest major station. Check current status before you travel.

faqs.q: Can I see Bhutan from Buxa Fort
faqs.a: The hills around Buxa rise to the Bhutan border, and from Lepchakha above the fort you look over the Dooars plains rather than into Bhutan's valleys. The old routes from Buxa into Bhutan are not open as tourist crossings; the nearest one for visitors is at Jaigaon–Phuentsholing.

Jigme Namgyal was the Trongsa Penlop, a powerful regional governor in central Bhutan, and one of the Bhutanese leaders during the Duar War of 1864–65. He was the father of Ugyen Wangchuck, who became the first King of Bhutan in 1907.
